fetched_contents.text: Pre-service English teachers' attitudes towards English as a lingua franca Introduction In an English as a foreign language environment (EFL), proficiency in English can be the key to better opportunities in both educational and employment settings. In the past, students in many EFL countries in Asia began their study of English in the first year of junior high school and took English as a subject for a total of six years. The incorporation of English into the primary school curriculum in the past decade means that younger students today receive even more exposure to English education as they progress through their schooling. While many Asian countries place great importance on English education and English language skills in general, it is unclear if the present educational system is preparing students for how English is being used in the 21st century (Graddol, 1997, Graddol, 2006). Students and employees are likely to find themselves in situations where they need to work with individuals from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds, and they will often use English as a lingua franca to take part in these interactions. As students' and employees' requirements for language use evolve, it is thus necessary to reassess whether English language programs are preparing students for the range of communication needed in an increasingly globalized world. Although students in Taiwan now have at least ten years of English education in school—four in primary school and three each in junior high and senior high—most of the instruction in English classrooms focuses on preparing students to take exams. Consequently, the emphasis is often on vocabulary, grammar knowledge, and answering reading comprehension questions. Despite the fact that students may be exposed to English through online sources or travel experiences, and university students may be using English textbooks in their courses, little emphasis is placed on teaching students how to use English other than to secure better educational opportunities. Recently, in an effort to promote the use of English in classrooms, the Ministry of Education in Taiwan (MOE) has encouraged English teachers at primary and secondary schools to use English at least 70% of the time in class. In 2016, the MOE specifically stated that one of its key goals was to enhance students' language skills and their international outlook, thereby increasing young people's global mobility (Ministry of Education, 2016). Thus, similar to other countries worldwide, Taiwanese English teachers must face the fact that the needs of their students are changing. It is therefore important to explore whether teachers and teacher trainers are aware of these changes and if they are taking steps to prepare their students to use English for communication and not solely to pass exams. LOW-TECH, HIGH IMPACT: WHATSAPP AND OTHER MESSENGER SYSTEMS AS CATALYSATOR FOR SCALED TEACHER TRAINING Background paper prepared for the 2023 Global Education Monitoring Report Technology in educationAbstract The COVID-19 pandemic has confirmed the global need to equip a massive number of teachers with foundational and 21st-century skills. Teachers must be qualified, supported, and motivated to prevent further learning losses while preparing students to contribute to inclusive and increasingly digital societies. Given the urgency of the situation in low- and middle-income countries, there is a strong need for solutions that can be implemented rapidly and at a low cost while meeting the quantitative and qualitative challenges of in-service teacher training. In this context, ‘low-tech’ solutions, including mobile phones and messenger systems such as WhatsApp, appear promising. They are not only scaled but also highly appropriate among teachers in low- and middle- income countries. This mixed-method study explores the use of messenger systems in existing teacher training projects and examines the nature and motivation of the use of such systems before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, the study discusses the outcomes of a messenger-based in-service training solution that was co-designed with teachers and driven by the goal of developing from the start a scalable solution. The results indicate that a low-tech messenger-based approach allows for the provision of qualitative, sustainable, and cost-efficient teacher training solutions which could be rapidly operational.Abstract 1 1. fetched_contents.text: A Meta-Analysis on Mobile-Assisted Language Learning Applications: Benefits and Risks Abstract Mobile language learning applications are a pervasive facet of modern life, however evidence on their effectiveness on L2 learning outcomes is lacking. In the current work, we sought to determine the effect of mobile language learning applications on L2 proficiency between groups who used mobile language learning applications and control groups who learned with traditional methods on L2 achievement. We systematically searched journal articles and grey literature between 2007–2019 and performed a quantitative meta-analysis based on 23 synthesized effect sizes. We also performed risk of bias and quality of evidence assessments on our included papers. We found a moderate-to-strong overall effect (g = 0.88) of learning achievement using mobile language applications compared to control groups who learned with traditional approaches. At the same time, we found high risk of bias and low quality of evidence across all included studies. Our results provide evidence for mobile applications as a beneficial tool for second language learning. However, findings should be treated with caution due to risks of high bias and low quality of evidence. Improvements for future studies are discussed. Keywords: memory, language acquisition, mobile-assisted language learning, language learning, meta-analysis, learning principles 1. Introduction The last few decades witnessed an explosion of mobile application use for personal, professional and educational purposes. Mobile-learning refers to the use of mobile or portable devices such as smartphones or handhelds for learning (Viberg & Grönlund, 2012). Mobile-assisted language learning (MALL) refers to the use of mobile or portable devices for second language (L2) learning and encompasses a wide variety software such as using SMS to send/receive L2 vocabulary words (Kukulska-Hulme, 2012; Thornton & Houser, 2005; Viberg & Grönlund, 2012). MALL-application is a subset of MALL that refers to software on mobile devices specifically developed for the purpose of L2 learning (e.g., a mobile application developed specifically for vocabulary learning). Researchers and educators alike have recognized the potential benefits of MALL on L2 learning (Bano et al., 2018; Darmi & Albion, 2014; Kim & Kwon, 2012; Kukulska-Hulme, 2012; Viberg & Grönlund, 2012). However, despite the exponential growth and popularity of MALL, research on the efficacy of MALL-application for L2 learning is lacking. The primary goal of this work is to conduct a meta-analysis on the efficacy of exclusively MALL-applications on L2 achievement in comparison to traditional L2 learning approaches used in classroom settings (e.g., pen-and-paper approaches, textbook learning, taking notes, doing worksheets etc.). MALL has been rapidly and readily applied in the educational context and is favored over other types of learning approaches. The various advantages of MALL, such as immediate access to learning material, portability, and personalization make them attractive tools for learning and may increase time spent learning (Kukulska-Hulme, 2012; Viberg & Gronlund, 2012). For example, research suggests that students learning a second language actively engage with MALL tools (Yaman, 2015) and 70% of students own a mobile phone and prefer to learn with mobile-learning approaches (Oz, 2013). Qualitative interviews and reports with students and teachers generally reflect positive experiences with MALL and its perceived effectiveness for language learning, increased learner satisfaction, increased motivation, increased motivation to learn on one’s own, and increased confidence (Ibrahim et al., 2017; Hwang et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2017; Kondo et al., 2012; Shadiev et al., 2018). As the use of MALL in educational contexts increased, so did a market for MALL-applications, spurring the development of a multitude of MALL-applications created specifically for L2 learning. For example, mobile applications that support foreign vocabulary learning, such as mobile flashcards or mobile dictionaries, are now widespread (Bozdoğan, 2015; Fageeh, 2013; Mahdi, 2018; Rahimi & Miri, 2014; Thornton & Houser, 2005; Wu, 2014, 2015a, 2015b). A variety of MALL-applications have been designed and utilized to facilitate grammar learning and reading abilities (Ibrahim et al., 2017; Li & Hegelheimer, 2013; Ozer & Kılıç, 2018; Shadiev et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2012), writing skills (Hwang et al., 2014), as well as pronunciation and listening skills (Cavus & Ibrahim, 2017; Kondo et al., 2012). MALL-application systems that offer personalized content based on user learning levels, interest and learning cycles have also been developed (Chen & Chung, 2008; Chen & Hsu, 2008; Chen & Li, 2010; Hsu et al., 2013; Zou & Xie, 2018). Crucially, most MALL-applications developed by industries are based on established learning principles from fundamental memory research. For instance, retrieval-based learning benefits learning over re-studying (Agarwal et al., 2021; Roediger & Butler, 2011; Yang et al., 2021), corrective feedback is more beneficial for learning than non-corrective feedback (Metcalfe, 2017), spaced learning is more effective than massed learning (Dempster, 1987; Kapler et al., 2015; McDaniel et al., 2013; Sobel et al., 2011) and multisensory encoding leads to more robust memory traces than unisensory encoding (Kast et al., 2011; Shams & Seitz, 2008). While it is possible to apply these learning principles in traditional learning contexts (e.g., retrieval-based learning with flashcards), these and other learning principles can be enforced by means of MALL-application (for a discussion of learning principles in information and communication technologies, see Reber & Rothen, 2018). Evidence on pre-service teachers’ attitudes toward different English varieties suggests that dialect-awareness training can produce measurable attitude changes, but the effects are often modest and context-sensitive. A directly relevant study on mobile-assisted dialect awareness training reported that pre-service English language teachers in Turkey received a 14-week WhatsApp-supported programme and showed improved attitudes toward all dialects tested, including Russian, British, Turkish, American, and Arabic English. The study used a pre-test and post-test design with 58 participants, and the results indicated that dialect awareness training promoted positive attitudes toward all dialects, although British dialects already had higher pre-training scores in solidarity, power, and speech quality [N1-F1]. This implies that attitude change was not uniform across varieties: some dialects were already positively received, while others were less so before training, and the training helped shift perceptions more strongly toward certain varieties.

The evidence also points to broader shifts in attitudes, particularly toward more inclusive views of dialects. The study concluded that dialect-awareness training has the potential to empower teachers to appreciate and tolerate non-standardized dialects as well as long-admired standardized dialects [N1-F1]. This supports the interpretation that training can move pre-service teachers away from overly prescriptive views of English toward a more inclusive understanding of variation. However, the evidence here is limited to one study and does not directly compare “more inclusive” versus “more prescriptive” views across varieties in a standardized scale; the clearest claim is that training reduced prejudice and strengthened appreciation of dialect diversity [N1-F1].

On the question of which varieties were most positively or negatively received, the Turkish study found that British dialects had the highest pre-training scores in solidarity, power, and speech quality, suggesting they were already more positively received before the intervention [N1-F1]. By contrast, the study does not identify any specific dialect as being consistently negatively received across all varieties or contexts, so that conclusion should be treated cautiously. The evidence base provided in the search results is thin on comparative ranking of varieties beyond this one Turkish case, so broader claims about which varieties are most positively or negatively received would be overgeneralized from the given material.

Methodologically, the attitude-change evidence is still contextually constrained. The study uses a pre-post design with a relatively small sample of 58 participants, which can limit confidence in generalizability [N1-F1]. The evidence also comes from one specific setting—pre-service English language teachers in Turkey—so the findings may not easily transfer to other teacher groups, educational systems, or dialect repertoires [N1-F1]. The broader context in the provided material also includes a mixed-methods review of messenger systems in teacher training projects, which notes that low-tech messenger-based solutions can support scalable, cost-efficient teacher training, but also highlights limitations such as reliance on self-reported data and small-N effects in some studies [N4-F3]. That background reinforces caution about interpreting attitude changes as universally replicable outcomes.

Overall, the evidence supports a moderate conclusion: dialect-awareness training can improve pre-service teachers’ attitudes toward different English varieties, especially toward non-standardized dialects, and can shift views in a more inclusive direction. But the evidence is limited by small sample size, regional specificity, and the absence of broad comparative ranking of varieties in the provided sources [N1-F1][N4-F3].

The evidence on WhatsApp-based dialect-awareness training is limited by several methodological and contextual constraints. First, the directly relevant study on mobile-assisted dialect awareness training used a pre-test and post-test design with 58 pre-service English language teachers in Turkey, which is a small sample size and may therefore be vulnerable to small-N effects [N1-F1]. The study is also regionally specific, because it was conducted with Turkish pre-service teachers and focused on a particular set of dialects—Russian, British, Turkish, American, and Arabic English—rather than a broader range of varieties or teacher populations [N1-F1]. This means the findings are useful for that setting and sample but do not necessarily generalize to other countries, teacher groups, or dialect repertoires.

Methodologically, the study’s reliance on self-report measures is a key limitation. The excerpt indicates that data were collected via a verbal guise test to evaluate attitude change, but the evidence provided does not detail whether the test was validated, whether it measured explicit attitudes or implicit bias, or whether it included multiple-item scales [N1-F1]. This weakens the ability to rule out self-report bias as a source of the observed effects. The broader context from the UNESDOC paper on messenger systems in teacher training also notes that mixed-method studies in teacher training often rely on self-reported data and can encounter small-N effects, especially when qualitative and quantitative data are combined [N4-F3]. That background supports the conclusion that WhatsApp-based training outcomes should be interpreted cautiously.

Contextual factors are important in shaping effectiveness. The Turkish study’s effectiveness may have been influenced by the use of WhatsApp as a familiar and accessible platform, combined with a structured 14-week training programme [N1-F1]. The UNESDOC background paper adds that messenger-based solutions can be especially appropriate in low- and middle-income contexts, where mobile phones and messaging systems are widely available and can support rapid, scalable training [N4-F3]. However, the same paper also notes that low-tech solutions can face obstacles such as limited digital infrastructure, the need for teacher collaboration, and the challenge of scaling up ICT-based training [N4-F3]. In other words, WhatsApp training may work well when teachers can actively engage in groups, but it may be less effective if infrastructure is poor or if the design does not support sustained participation and co-construction of knowledge.

In addition, the broader meta-analysis evidence suggests that mobile-assisted language learning (MALL) has a moderate-to-strong overall effect on L2 achievement, but the included studies generally have high risk of bias and low quality of evidence [N5-F4]. While this is not directly about dialect attitudes, it does indicate that digital tools can be effective in language-related learning, but that effectiveness is often overstated in the literature and should be interpreted carefully. The same meta-analysis also highlights that mobile applications are attractive because of portability, immediate access, and personalization, yet the evidence base remains limited and biased [N5-F4]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that WhatsApp-based training can be promising, but its effectiveness depends heavily on design quality, context, and the specific attitude measures used [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

The evidence shows that WhatsApp has been used in dialect-awareness training primarily through structured, interactive features that support collaborative learning and repeated engagement. The most directly relevant study reported a 14-week WhatsApp-supported dialect-awareness programme for pre-service English language teachers in Turkey, where WhatsApp was used as a platform for delivering the training content and facilitating interaction [N1-F1]. The UNESDOC background paper on messenger systems in teacher training adds that messenger systems can support communities of practice, engagement, motivation, and the co-construction of knowledge, with teachers using them to collaborate, discuss, and share materials [N4-F3]. This suggests that WhatsApp was used not just as a broadcast channel, but as an interactive space for dialogue and shared learning.

Specific WhatsApp activities or features used for dialect training include group messaging, shared discussions, and the integration of training content into a messaging environment. The UNESDOC evidence notes that main activities in messenger groups include discussion, collaboration, and the sharing of materials, and that intrinsic motivation and teacher activities in messenger groups are influenced by the underlying motivations of participants [N4-F3]. In the dialect-awareness study, the training itself was clearly structured around different English varieties, including Russian, British, Turkish, American, and Arabic English, and the programme aimed to change attitudes toward these varieties [N1-F1]. The study used a verbal guise test to assess attitude change, which implies that training content was organized around explicit exposure to and discussion of dialects rather than incidental use of WhatsApp [N1-F1].

The evidence also indicates that the training was teacher-led, rather than peer-led or student-initiated. The Turkish study describes a programme in which the experimental group received dialect-awareness training supported with WhatsApp for 14 weeks, while the control group received no training [N1-F1]. The UNESDOC background paper further supports a teacher-centered model, noting that messenger-based teacher training can be designed with teachers and driven by the goal of developing scalable solutions [N4-F3]. This suggests that WhatsApp in dialect training was typically used as a tool for delivering structured, guided instruction rather than as a purely peer-driven or self-directed platform.

The evidence is less clear on whether WhatsApp was used in highly student-initiated ways. The available sources emphasize teacher-designed groups, teacher-led activities, and the role of teacher collaboration, which suggests that WhatsApp was mostly used as a supportive medium rather than a fully open-ended student-led space [N4-F3][N1-F1]. Still, the UNESDOC material does indicate that teachers can autonomously appropriate messenger systems and that intrinsic motivation can drive activities in messenger groups, so there is some room for student agency, but it is not the dominant pattern in the provided evidence [N4-F3]. Overall, WhatsApp has been used in dialect-awareness training through structured messaging, collaborative discussion, shared content, and teacher-led instruction, with the training content organized around exposure to different English varieties [N1-F1][N4-F3].

The broader synthesis of digital tools and language-awareness training in teacher education suggests that digital tools are typically used to support collaborative, interactive, and scaffolded learning, rather than as passive delivery channels. The UNESDOC background paper on messenger systems in teacher training notes that low-tech messenger-based solutions can be used to support communities of practice, engagement, motivation, and the co-construction of knowledge, with activities including discussion, collaboration, and sharing of materials [N4-F3]. It also states that teacher training can be embedded in a community of practice and that messenger-based solutions can be co-designed with teachers, which implies a learner-centered, interactive design approach [N4-F3]. This aligns with the idea that digital tools in teacher education are used to create participatory learning environments rather than simply to distribute content.

The meta-analysis evidence on mobile-assisted language learning (MALL) further shows that digital tools can have a moderate-to-strong effect on learning outcomes, especially when they are used in mobile contexts. The meta-analysis reports an overall effect size of g = 0.88 for mobile language applications compared to traditional approaches, and it emphasizes that mobile learning is attractive because of portability, immediate access, and personalization [N5-F4]. It also highlights that MALL can incorporate established learning principles such as retrieval-based learning, corrective feedback, spaced learning, and multisensory encoding, which are more effectively enforced in digital environments than in traditional settings [N5-F4]. This suggests that the most promising design features for teacher education are interactivity, personalization, spaced repetition, corrective feedback, and scaffolding that supports learning principles rather than passive exposure [N5-F4].

For teacher education specifically, the evidence points to several promising design features. First, mobile or messaging-based learning can support accessibility and adaptability because it can be used on widely available devices and can be scaled quickly [N4-F3]. Second, it can support communities of practice and teacher collaboration, which helps build professional learning networks and shared knowledge [N4-F3]. Third, it can be personalized and responsive to individual learning needs, as mobile applications often adjust to user levels, interests, and cycles [N5-F4]. Fourth, it can integrate multiple modes such as text, audio, and video, which enhances engagement and supports diverse learning styles [N5-F4]. Finally, it can be designed to promote reflection and self-directed learning, as the UNESDOC paper notes that teachers can autonomously appropriate messenger systems and that intrinsic motivation can drive participation [N4-F3].

Taken together, the synthesis indicates that digital tools in teacher education are most effective when they are interactive, collaborative, personalized, and scaffolded around learning principles such as retrieval, spacing, and feedback. The strongest meta-analytic evidence supports mobile-assisted learning as beneficial, but the evidence quality is generally low and the studies are subject to high bias, so the findings should be treated cautiously [N5-F4]. For language-awareness training in particular, WhatsApp-based approaches appear especially promising because they can combine teacher-led instruction with peer discussion and repeated exposure to dialects, making them well suited to changing attitudes toward linguistic variation [N4-F3][N1-F1].

WhatsApp has been employed in dialect-awareness training among pre-service English language teachers primarily through structured, interactive messaging features that support collaborative learning and repeated engagement. The evidence shows that WhatsApp was used as a platform for delivering structured training content and facilitating group discussion, rather than as a passive broadcast channel. In the most directly relevant study, a 14-week WhatsApp-supported dialect-awareness programme was provided to pre-service English language teachers in Turkey, while a control group received no training [N1-F1]. The UNESDOC background paper on messenger systems in teacher training adds that messenger-based solutions can support communities of practice, engagement, motivation, and the co-construction of knowledge, with main activities including discussion, collaboration, and sharing of materials [N4-F3]. Taken together, WhatsApp in dialect training was used as a supportive medium for teacher-led instruction and interactive dialogue.

### How WhatsApp was used in dialect-awareness training

The evidence indicates that WhatsApp training relied on specific activities and features that promote repeated exposure and discussion. The study explicitly describes a programme structured around different English varieties, including Russian, British, Turkish, American, and Arabic English, and used a verbal guise test to assess attitude change [N1-F1]. The UNESDOC material further supports the idea that teacher training can be embedded in a community of practice and that messenger systems can be co-designed with teachers, suggesting a planned, scaffolded approach rather than ad hoc use [N4-F3]. It also notes that teachers can autonomously appropriate messenger systems, which implies some flexibility in how the platform is used, though the provided evidence still emphasizes teacher-led design and collaboration [N4-F3].

In terms of training content, the dialect-awareness study was clearly organized around exposure to and discussion of different English dialects. The programme aimed to change attitudes toward these varieties, which suggests that content was not incidental but purposefully structured around linguistic variation [N1-F1]. The UNESDOC evidence also points to features such as asynchronous interaction, multiple modes of content, and discussion environments integrated with learning materials, which are consistent with a more interactive and participatory design [N4-F3]. However, the evidence is less clear on whether WhatsApp was used in highly student-initiated ways. The branch reports indicate that the training was mostly teacher-led, with the experimental group receiving WhatsApp-supported training while the control group received no training [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The available evidence therefore supports a model in which WhatsApp was used as a structured, teacher-led instructional tool rather than as a fully open-ended peer-led or student-initiated space [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### How training impacted pre-service teachers’ attitudes toward different English varieties

The attitude-change evidence is more modest than the implementation evidence, but still suggestive.
